title: Hosted API streaming backpressure and param tuning demo
meeting_header:
Date: 2026-03-20
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Asha Patel (Stonebridge), Tom Hargreaves (Stonebridge), Maya Chen (Stonebridge)
summary: AE + SE walked Stonebridge through Hosted API streaming behavior, backpressure controls, and parameter tuning (max_tokens, temperature, top_p, streaming chunking). Demo included simulated burst traffic and retry/backoff patterns. Customer cares about predictable tail latency for chat and avoiding over-costly token usage. Next steps: run a 1k-message benchmark, share security & pricing docs, schedule a deeper private deployment conversation.
topics: Backpressure and client-side vs server-side strategies
Param tuning: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences
action_items: Marco Ruiz: run 1k-message streaming benchmark with Stonebridge prompt set and share results (due 2026-03-27)
Lena Park: send hosted pricing tiers and burst pricing examples (due 2026-03-22)
Marco Ruiz: provide sample client retry library snippets (JS + Python) and note idempotency guidance (due 2026-03-24)
Stonebridge (Asha): share representative prompt set and tail-latency SLOs (due 2026-03-23)
next_steps: Marco to run benchmark and upload results to shared folder
Lena to email pricing + security slide deck
Schedule follow-up deep dive on private deployment if benchmarks meet SLOs
Stonebridge to review security docs and confirm stakeholders for procurement
transcript:
00:00 - Lena Park: alright everyone thanks for joining we've got about 50 minutes carved out for aHosted API streaming demo focused on backpressure and param tuning, we're gonna cover behavioral patterns and then run a short sim.
00:12 - Tom Hargreaves: sounds good, keen to understand tail latency under bursts, that's our biggest worry.
00:18 - Lena Park: yeah totally, especially for multi-turn chat right, latency spikes cost you conversions. Marco will lead the demo but quick intro: Redwood hosted api supports streaming tokens, chunked frames, and we have server-side batching and prefix caching.
00:35 - Marco Ruiz: hey all, hi Maya, Asha, Tom. I'm gonna kick off with a quick topology slide then jump into a live curl + Node example.
00:50 - Asha Patel: quick q, Stonebridge runs a chat system that needs sub-200ms response for short answers and sub-second for long form, is that realistic on hosted?
00:59 - Marco Ruiz: short answers definitely in many regions with the right model and batching disabled for low latency. For longer outputs we recommend streaming with a small chunk size and prefix cache to reduce repeated compute.
01:14 - Marco Ruiz: showing the console now — per-route latency histograms, token breakdown, streaming lag metric. You can see tail at p95/p99, and Optimize suggests turning on prefix caching for repeated prompts.
01:30 - Maya Chen: when you say chunk size, what controls that? client-side chunk read or server-side?
01:36 - Marco Ruiz: good question. Client sees server-chunked frames. We expose stream chunk size and recommend the client buffer to handle partial frames. There's also a 'stream_delta_ms' in some SDKs, but practically you tune 'max_output_tokens' and server chunking to reduce latencies.
01:50 - Tom Hargreaves: is there backpressure? if our workers suddenly spike to 10k concurrent users, do requests queue? what's the behavior?
01:59 - Marco Ruiz: Redwood has multi-layer backpressure: autoscaling pools on Dedicated but for Hosted we do graceful shedding and routing. For single request bursts, server will queue up to a soft limit then return 429s with Retry-After. We recommend exponential backoff on client side with jitter and idempotency tokens to avoid duplicate charges.
02:20 - Lena Park: to add, Optimize can recommend batch sizes and quantization profiles per workload — for you given medical notes generation, we suggested accuracy-first tuning.
02:31 - Asha Patel: medical notes, yes. we also have PHI concerns. can you quickly summarize data retention and logging?
02:40 - Lena Park: quick summary: Hosted API has configurable retention, SSO + org-level retention policies, and we provide SOC2 Type II report. For strict requirements you can use Private which keeps logs in your VPC. I'll send the security pack after call.
02:56 - Marco Ruiz: demo time — I'll run a synthetic 100 concurrent stream using our node client. pointing browser to the curl output.
03:10 - Speaker 1: (muffled) — Marco's sharing a terminal.
03:18 - Marco Ruiz: okay starting now — you might see token chunks come in roughly every 80ms for this model. watch the p95 metric in the console.
04:05 - Maya Chen: hmm I'm seeing some partial frames drop in the test harness — is that expected?
04:12 - Marco Ruiz: could be client buffer timeout, sometimes websockets timeout on idle frames; we often recommend keepalive pings or smaller chunk windows. Also note transcription sometimes reports KV cache as KV cash in transcripts ha.
04:28 - Tom Hargreaves: sorry can you repeat the retry guidance? we want idempotency so we don't double-charge a payment gateway call triggered by assistant.
04:36 - Marco Ruiz: yes use an idempotency token per user turn, and store last-token per conversation. Retries: exponential backoff starting at 200ms, doubling with full jitter, cap at 5s and 3 retries for streaming endpoints. If you need stronger guarantees, use the 'generate' endpoint with server-side dedupe.
05:00 - Asha Patel: about token cost — how can we avoid accidental runaway generations? stop sequences? max tokens?
05:07 - Marco Ruiz: use both. Set a conservative max_output_tokens on the request, provide explicit stop sequences, and use the generation_cost_limit in console to guard. Optimize can flag prompts that blow past expected token counts during evals.
05:25 - Lena Park: quick interjection — earlier you mentioned private deploys, if you decide on Private we can keep the inference inside your VPC and plug into your KMS for keying.
05:35 - Tom Hargreaves: we'd probably try hosted for initial pilot though, cheaper ops. how much control over model selection do we have?
05:41 - Marco Ruiz: you can pin model versions per route, route by latency/cost, and set fallbacks to a cheaper quantized model. That helps maintain availability if higher-tier model hits capacity.
05:53 - Maya Chen: in the demo I noticed a spike in p99 when the node benchmark hit 400 concurrent streams, is that a product limitation?
06:00 - Marco Ruiz: that was expected — with concurrency at that level, continuous batching increases per-token latency. You can mitigate with smaller per-request batch caps or assign a dedicated pool. For hosted we do best-effort but at enterprise scale Dedicated offers reserved capacity.
06:18 - Marco Ruiz: starting a second test — burst to 1k short requests to observe 429 behavior.
06:40 - Asha Patel: hey a small nit, the transcript shows some words wrong sometimes — you mentioned that earlier, it's fine.
06:45 - Marco Ruiz: yeah auto-transcription not perfect. back to the burst — as requests exceeded soft queue you'll see 429s emitted and client-saw Retry-After header set to 30s in this test.
07:05 - Tom Hargreaves: 30s seems long, can that be configured?
07:10 - Marco Ruiz: Retry-After is based on current capacity pressure and region. We can't expose direct retry-after tuning for hosted, but Dedicated gives you stronger controls on the autoscaler and lower Retry-After. Also plan for client-side backoff to smooth retries.
07:25 - Maya Chen: in practice our UX team cares about showing partial responses as soon as available, how do you recommend handling streaming partials + fallbacks?
07:34 - Marco Ruiz: render deltas as they arrive, show a spinner for server-side continuation. If you switch to fallback model mid-generation we send a final delta and a special 'fallback' meta-chunk. Client should be able to handle mid-stream model swaps.
07:50 - Lena Park: demo note — we'll share the sample SDK that already handles fallback markers.
08:00 - Marco Ruiz: moving on to param tuning. temperature controls randomness; at 0.0 near deterministic, 0.7 creative, 1.2 high variance. For clinical notes we recommend 0.0-0.2. top_p and temperature are interchangeable in effect but top_p 0.9 is often safe.
08:24 - Asha Patel: do you have recommended defaults for multi-turn where we keep some assistant history and system prompts?
08:30 - Marco Ruiz: yes use shorter system prompts and selectively include only the last N turns to keep token counts low. Use KV cache on long context where possible — note that KV cache reduces re-encoding cost but can complicate privacy guarantees if shared.
08:46 - Tom Hargreaves: what about rate limits—are there per-org vs per-route limits?
08:50 - Lena Park: hosted has tiered quotas per account and route-level limits you can configure. We can also set soft quotas and alerts in the console.
09:00 - Marco Ruiz: show the example retry snippet now — Node and Python. (reads code) using axios/fetch we pass headers: Idempotency-Key, and on 429/5xx we backoff with 200ms base + jitter. Here's the sample link: https://redwood.example.com/demo/streaming-retries-snippets
09:25 - Maya Chen: that'll be helpful, could you include go snippets? our backend team prefers go.
09:29 - Marco Ruiz: sure — we'll add Go.
09:33 - Asha Patel: can you show the Optimize recommendations quickly? we want to lower cost without harming accuracy.
09:38 - Marco Ruiz: switching to Optimize tab — it has workload profiling. For your prompt set it suggests: 1) enable prefix caching for repeated templates; 2) reduce max_tokens from 512 to 256 for short notes; 3) try quantized v2-small for non-critical assistant tasks. All suggestions show estimated delta in token cost.
09:58 - Tom Hargreaves: how accurate are those estimates?
10:02 - Marco Ruiz: they're based on sampled runs and tokenization distributions — good heuristic but we recommend running a benchmark.
10:10 - Marco Ruiz: starting the benchmark now — synthetic prompt set of 500 messages with mixed short/long. I'll stream metrics to console.
12:45 - Speaker 2: (typing) — metrics look stable so far.
13:05 - Marco Ruiz: benchmark done — p95 looks at 420ms for short responses, p99 1.2s under this model, and about 8% of requests hit token spike > expected. We'll share full CSV.
13:28 - Asha Patel: 1.2s p99 is borderline but maybe acceptable for now. we want to see how it moves with concurrency.
13:34 - Marco Ruiz: agree. I'll run the 1k-message test after the call and share results.
13:40 - Lena Park: quick pause — any regulatory blockers for hosted with PHI?
13:46 - Tom Hargreaves: our legal needs to see SOC2 and data flow diagrams.
13:50 - Lena Park: understood we have an SOC2 pack. I'll attach it. For PHI we often recommend Private or a hybrid where inference runs in Private and audit logs flow to your SIEM.
14:05 - Maya Chen: procurement timeline — if pilot is successful, we might move to procurement in 6–8 weeks.
14:10 - Lena Park: great, that aligns with doing a 2–4 week pilot.
14:20 - Marco Ruiz: one more technical note — streaming with small chunks increases network overhead. If clients have really noisy connections, you may want slightly larger chunk sizes to amortize RTTs.
14:36 - Asha Patel: that makes sense, we have some mobile clients with flaky connections.
14:42 - Marco Ruiz: also think about partial response reconciliation on client — keep a stable message id.
14:50 - Tom Hargreaves: are there known differences in behavior between models? like hallucination rates during streaming?
14:56 - Marco Ruiz: hallucinations are model-dependent, streaming doesn't inherently increase hallucination but partial decoding and early termination can lead to incomplete outputs. Use evals tied to prompts to surface regressions.
15:10 - Lena Park: ok we're about halfway through the time — any other high-level Qs?
15:15 - Maya Chen: just one: can the console produce alerts when token spend per-route spikes?
15:20 - Marco Ruiz: yes alerts and budget caps per route, email/Slack integrations.
15:27 - Asha Patel: demo of an SDK upload? we want to see how quick it is to drop in.
15:33 - Marco Ruiz: sure, I'll run a tiny code drop — show package install and sample call. (runs) It takes about 2 minutes to wire.
16:10 - Marco Ruiz: starting the 1k-message headless run now — this will run after the call and I'll attach results in the shared folder, CSV + consolidated console link.
16:25 - Tom Hargreaves: perfect. regarding retries again, if we get partial responses and then retry is there a risk of duplicated content to end user?
16:33 - Marco Ruiz: yes if you re-emit tokens you'll duplicate. We recommend client reconcilers that resume from last-acknowledged token index or issue a fresh turn with idempotency. The SDKs include helpers for resumption.
16:50 - Lena Park: ok let's recap next steps and owners — Marco runs benchmark, Lena sends security + pricing, Stonebridge shares prompt set.
17:02 - Maya Chen: can we get an example SLA for hosted pilot?
17:07 - Lena Park: yes we'll provide a pilot SLA doc.
17:12 - Asha Patel: one last ask: can you show how fallbacks look in the event of model throttling?
17:18 - Marco Ruiz: brief demo — triggering fallback to a quantized variant. (shares) Client receives a fallback meta chunk and final delta; we also emit a console event for audit.
17:48 - Tom Hargreaves: good — that helps our ops team.
17:52 - Lena Park: ok wrapping up. I'll email the deck, security pack, pricing, and the node/python/go snippets. Marco will run the 1k-message sim and post results by Friday.
18:05 - Maya Chen: thanks everyone, very useful.
18:10 - Marco Ruiz: thanks all.
18:15 - Lena Park: bye all, we'll follow up via email.
52:00 - (call ended)
